articles.title_orig: Nvidia CEO investigated in China spy scandal
articles.title_zh: Nvidia CEO investigated in China spy scandal
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said he had spoken to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang earlier Monday after Nvidia revealed late Sunday that it had launched an investigation into his extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump called Huang “to see if he’s feeling all right,” the president said at an impromptu news briefing.
“He had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy,” Trump said of Huang, adding, “I really believe him.”
“We’ll look into it,” said the president. “I know the FBI is looking into it, in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape.”
The Justice Department is conducting a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, the Singaporean company suspected of smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China, according to a source familiar with the matter who spoke to NBC News.
Megaspeed is the data center company at the center of the controversy involving Huang, who is said to have had a relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, the woman who U.S. intelligence officials now believe to be a Chinese spy. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are not related.
The investigation is focused on the role of Megaspeed in allegedly shipping Nvidia artificial intelligence computer chips to customers in China, which would violate strict U.S. export controls on those chips.
In addition to Megaspeed, the probe is looking at people tied to the company like Alice Huang, and at whether she was recruited by China to spy and assist the smuggling of the AI chips into China.
The investigation is being led by the department’s National Security Division, in conjunction with the FBI and the Bureau of Industry and Security, the investigative division of the Commerce Department.
On Sunday, the Nvidia board announced it was “initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
At the same time, Jensen Huang announced that he had been “unfaithful to my wife,” while also apologizing to Nvidia employees.
“I was amazed, because I view him as a very high-quality person,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “He’s an amazing guy. I hope there’s no problem.”
Trump indicated for the second time in as many days that he wanted Huang to remain the leader of Nvidia, the second-largest public company in the world. “I hope there’s no problem. If there is a problem, we’ll let you know about it. But I hope there’s no problem.”
Nvidia spokespeople did not immediately reply to a request for comment Monday following Trump’s remarks. Nvidia previously said Huang would remain CEO, despite the revelations.
The Justice Department also declined to comment on the matter.
Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that “the so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China.”
Shares of Nvidia closed down 4.2% in Monday’s trading, bucking overall market momentum. The stock was the worst-performing company in the Dow and the Nasdaq.
The news surrounding Nvidia and Huang has also drawn intense congressional scrutiny.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., on Monday called for “a full briefing” on the issues engulfing Nvidia. Jeffries is likely to be elected the next speaker of the House in January.
Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Jim Banks, R-Ind., also said in a joint statement that Congress should “take decisive action” regarding oversight of AI-linked companies.
The disclosures by Nvidia and Huang “makes these national security concerns even more urgent and raises important questions NVIDIA must answer,” Warren and Banks wrote.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.
Michael Kosnar is the Justice Department Producer for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Man who sent racist threats to UK Conservative leader Badenoch receives jail sentence
articles.title_zh: Man who sent racist threats to UK Conservative leader Badenoch receives jail sentence
articles.content_orig:
A man has been jailed for sending the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch emails threatening to shoot her dead.
Ex-teacher Kieran Kyle sent three emails on 2 May to the Tory party leader in which he made racist references and claimed to have been in the IRA, the court heard.
The 43-year-old, from Gillingham in Kent, pleaded guilty on 22 September at Westminster Magistrates' Court to two counts of sending communications of an indecent or offensive nature.
Kyle was sentenced to 20 weeks in prison at the same court on Monday.
In a victim impact statement read to the court, Badenoch and her husband Hamish said the "malicious communications and targeted harassment" not only had an effect on them, but also undermined "a healthy democracy".
In two of the emails, Kyle had made racist references and written: "I'm ex-IRA, so Bloody Sunday references from you are going to give you trouble," the court heard.
The messages were sent on the day Badenoch apologised for footage from Bloody Sunday being mistakenly used in a social media clip to criticise a parliamentary Bill on legacy issues in Northern Ireland.
The Tory leader had said she did not sign off the video and that it was sent out by "very young people".
The video criticising the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill, posted to her social media channels on 28 April, showed Badenoch saying the Labour legislation would "drag" Troubles veterans back to court.
Thirteen unarmed civilians were shot dead when members of the Army's Parachute Regiment opened fire on civil rights demonstrators in the Bogside area of Londonderry on 30 January 1972, a date that became known as Bloody Sunday.
The court heard Kyle had also sent an email to Badenoch's husband Hamish on 29 April, which used a racist term and said she had a "big mouth" and he should "put a leash on her".
Prosecutor Ben Holt said the North West Essex MP and her husband were left "distressed" and "upset", particularly by the "racist language and threats of violence used towards them".
He added Cheryl Bacon, head of Badenoch's parliamentary office, said the emails were "disgusting" and "distressing" to read.
Baiju Thittala, defending, told the court Kyle "did not know" who Badenoch was at the time of the offences, adding "he only realised later, once he had sent the emails".
Asked by the judge how Kyle, a former secondary school teacher, could not know who Badenoch was, Thittala said: "He just 'Googled' it and it came up as the opposition leader."
The judge said: "The first emails were sent to Mr Badenoch, so I don't think he did not appreciate who Mrs Badenoch was.
"So he clearly knew who Mrs Badenoch was because he researched her husband's details first."
The Badenochs said in their victim impact statement: "Our primary concern arising from this offence is not the personal impact on us, but the wider consequences that malicious communications and targeted harassment have on our democratic life.
"When individuals choose to intimidate, threaten, or aggressively target elected representatives or public figures, the harm extends far beyond any single person. It undermines a healthy democracy."
The continued: "Public service relies on people being willing to step forward, often at significant personal cost, to represent their communities and contribute to public life.
"Increasingly, however, those who do so face hostility, harassment, and attempts to silence or intimidate them."
The judge also handed Kyle a restraining order, meaning he cannot contact Badenoch, her husband or her parliamentary office for five years.

articles.title_zh: California amusement park to close after more than 50 years
articles.content_orig:
The steel roller coaster is set for a comeback after Six Flags acquired the attraction from the now-closed Fun Spot America Atlanta. (Credit: American Coaster Enthusiasts)
A California amusement park will close its gates for the final time next year after more than 50 seasons in business.
California’s Great America, owned by Six Flags, in Santa Clara said it will cease operations after it opted not to extend its land lease that expires in June 2028.
The park’s final season will begin in March 2027 and end on Labor Day.
SIX FLAGS GIVES FAN-FAVORITE ARIEFORCE ONE COASTER A SECOND LIFE
The Patriot roller coaster takes riders through a 360-degree loop during a preview ride at California's Great America amusement park in Santa Clara, California. (Anda Chu/Bay Area News Group via Getty Images)
"The Farewell Season is an opportunity for generations of Bay Area guests to return, spend time with family and friends, and revisit the attractions and traditions that have made the park in Santa Clara, California such a meaningful part of the community," said Dave Vosejpka , park manager of California's Great America.
The closure marks the end of an era that began in 1976, when the park opened as Marriott’s Great America. It operated for decades on public land until former owner Cedar Fair Entertainment Co. purchased the 112 acres underneath the park in 2019 for around $150 million.
The closure marks the end of an era that began in 1976. (Kimberly White/Getty Images for California's Great America)
SIX FLAGS TO SELL 7 AMUSEMENT PARKS IN DEAL WORTH MORE THAN $330M
Cedar Fair sold the land three years later to real estate company Prologis for around $310 million with a lease agreement. Cedar Fair merged with Six Flags in 2024.
Signs of a shutdown had surfaced over the past few years. Great America canceled most live entertainment and its Halloween and Christmas events last year, according to the Los Angeles Times.
The closure of Great America comes after parent company Six Flags sold seven parks to EPR Properties earlier this year.

articles.title_orig: Security Levels At U.S. Bases In England Raised Without Explanation
articles.title_zh: Security Levels At U.S. Bases In England Raised Without Explanation
articles.content_orig:
At least two bases in England hosting U.S. Air Force aircraft are operating under beefed-up security protocols, a U.S. official told us Monday afternoon. The official was responding to our questions about what appeared to be unusual aircraft movements out of RAF Mildenhall. It is unclear what spurred these measures, how long they have been in place or whether they are connected to an ongoing investigation into whether Iran was behind a security incident at RAF Fairford in September that reportedly prompted the hasty departure of B-1 Lancer bombers.
“Enhanced force protection measures are in effect across RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall,” the official told us. “We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families. We are working closely with our host nation counterparts to minimize impacts from enhanced force protection activities and ensure the safety of U.S. personnel, their families and the local community.”
The official declined to say what steps were taken.
“For operational security reasons, we do not discuss specific force protection measures,” the official added.
RAF Mildenhall and RAF Lakenheath are both major hubs for the U.S. Air Force. Mildenhall’s host unit is the 100th Air Refueling Wing, which operates KC-135 Stratotanker aerial refueling jets. The base is also home to Air Force RC-135V/W Rivet Joint reconnaissance aircraft , Air Force Special Operations Command (AFSOC) CV-22 Osprey tiltrotor aircraft and MC-130J Commando II special operations cargo planes . Lakenheath hosts Air Force F-15E Strike Eagle and F-35A Lightning II aircraft .
Both bases also see frequent flights transiting to other locations.
As we noted earlier in this piece, the official was responding to our questions about unusual aircraft movements out of Mildenhall. They were first noticed by the @DefenceGeek open-source flight tracker account.
“Over the course of today, a number of US Air Force assets at RAF Mildenhall (EGUN) have made unannounced/unexpected movements to other locations, with several of those movements in motion presently,” DefenceGeek wrote on X. “The initial few this morning I assumed were due to heavy fog in the area, but other information is now suggesting something else… – Several KC-135s have moved to Spangdahlem (ETAD) or Prestwick (EGPK) – CV-22Bs have moved from Mildenhall to Lakenheath It remains unclear if there is an ongoing exercise or information of a potential threat (following the incident at RAF Fairford)…”
UPDATE: US Assets at RAF Mildenhall Dispersing For those commenting and asking, no, the NOTAMs regarding RAF Mildenhall are not related to what is currently going on. The two NOTAMs are for Veterans Day (Wednesday) and Thanksgiving (end of November). Today's situation does not…
DefenceGeek also noted that RAF Lakenheath posted a notice this morning on Facebook urging vigilance in spotting and reporting drones.
US Assets at RAF Mildenhall Dispersing? Over the course of today, a number of US Air Force assets at RAF Mildenhall (EGUN) have made unannounced/unexpected movements to other locations, with several of those movements in motion presently. The initial few this morning I assumed… pic.twitter.com/vVVA0cRljN
“Our strongest security asset is an observant community,” the RAF Lakenheath Facebook post read . “Staying vigilant and reporting suspicious activity, including unauthorized drone activity, helps protect our Airmen, families and mission. If you see something unusual on or around the Tri-Base area, report it to Security Forces.”
It is unclear what connection, if any, the Lakenheath post has to the enhanced force protection status. U.S. Air Forces in Europe – Air Forces Africa (USAFE) declined to discuss security measures. The command oversees U.S. Air Force operations in Europe and Africa.
“U.S. Air Force aircraft rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons including training and real world requirements,” USAFE told us. “U.S. military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our Allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets.”
The departures from Mildenhall took place amid an ongoing flow of refueling tankers and other aircraft to the Middle East as President Donald Trump continues to mull whether to resume strikes against Iran . This afternoon, Trump wrapped up his meeting with Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani to discuss a flagging effort to resolve the conflict with Iran through diplomacy.
It should also be noted that in late November 2024, Lakenheath, Mildenhall and two other RAF bases hosting U.S. forces experienced drone incursions, which we were the first to write about .
As we mentioned earlier in this piece, security concerns about bases in England hosting U.S. Air Force aircraft and personnel were raised following an incident at RAF Fairford.
Like Mildenhall and Lakenheath, RAF Fairford is a major hub for U.S. military aircraft in the United Kingdom. It is a regular host of strategic assets, including bombers and U-2 spy planes. It also acts as a pit stop for other aircraft, including fighters, that are being ferried to and from the United States. Bomber strikes launched from Fairford were a central aspect of major U.S. combat operations against Iran earlier this year.
In late September, five men were arrested on suspicion of driving bomb-laden vans toward it. They were soon released on bail after no explosives were found, but two men were later arrested, one of who “charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, which police earlier said they believed to be Iran,” according to the BBC .
A week after the security incident , U.S. Air Force B-1B Lancer bombers that had been deployed to RAF Fairford in the U.K. since Operation Epic Fury returned to their home stations, a U.S. defense official confirmed to TWZ at the time. The hasty movement was reportedly sparked by new Iranian threats against the base. As we previously reported , Tehran directly threatened RAF Fairford in July over its use as a base to launch attacks against Iran.
We can’t say for sure what prompted the enhanced security at RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall or whether the aircraft movements at Mildenhall are precautionary or just normal shifting of resources. We will continue to monitor the situation and provide updates when warranted.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow Pushes 1000 Points Higher, Nvidia Stock Slides Over Jensen Huang Affair Probe
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow Pushes 1000 Points Higher, Nvidia Stock Slides Over Jensen Huang Affair Probe
articles.content_orig:
U.S. stock futures largely traded near the flatline Monday night as traders awaited a pivotal consumer inflation report.
S&P 500 futures were marginally higher, while futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average were up 45 points. Nasdaq-100 futures added 0.2%.
During the regular trading day, the Dow Industrials gained 1,104 points, or 2.2%, while the S&P 500 popped about 2.4%. The Nasdaq Composite rose 2.7%. Monday's rally came after a rocky week for markets, in which traders grew concerned of an impending slowdown in data center buildouts after Democrats posted big victories in the midterm elections.
While the tech sector rebounded in Monday's regular trading, Nvidia sat out the rally.
Shares of the chipmaker slid 4% after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials, according to The New York Times, say is a spy for China's Ministry of State Security. The company's board of directors also launched an independent internal investigation , pointing to recent reporting that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."
Oil prices also fell on Monday, lending the market support. The U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures settled down more than 4%, while Brent crude futures slid more than 5%.
Investors are awaiting the October consumer price index report due on Tuesday. Economists polled by Dow Jones see headline CPI growing at a rate of 0.3% and core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy costs, rising 0.2% from the prior month.
This would mark a deceleration from September's readings, when headline CPI grew 0.6% and core CPI advanced 0.3%.
"We think the slowdown in core CPI will stem from a reversion of shelter prices, primarily owners' equivalent rents and lodging away from home. Similarly, the stabilization in diesel prices should help to quell price pressures in energy-intensive goods," wrote Christopher Hodge, chief economist of the U.S. at Natixis CIB Americas.
Annual figures will not be provided for Tuesday's report because of the 2025 government shutdown. At that time, the Bureau of Labor Statistics was unable to collect some data which means there isn't a comparable figure for the index.
Stock futures traded near the flatline on Monday.
S&P 500 futures gained just 0.07%, while Dow Jones Industrial Average futures rose 12 points, or 0.02%. Nasdaq-100 futures were up 0.19%.

articles.title_orig: Boeing to cut 5% of commercial jet workforce amid production struggles
articles.title_zh: Boeing to cut 5% of commercial jet workforce amid production struggles
articles.content_orig:
Boeing said Monday that it plans to cut 5% of its commercial airplane workforce as its production ramp-up is moving at a slower pace than the company expected.
The cuts will be through a combination of attrition and layoffs, Stephanie Pope, head of the commercial aircraft unit, said in a memo to staff.
Pope reiterated that the company is still working to stabilize production rates of its bestselling 737 Max planes, which are made outside of Seattle.
CEO Kelly Ortberg told investors last month that the company won't significantly increase production of the Max aircraft until the second half of next year. He said the company's wing production has been slower than expected.
"Adjusting our production schedules and reducing aircraft output puts us in an overstaffed position," Pope said in her note Monday. "Unfortunately, that means we need to align our staffing levels to our revised business plan, resulting in a reduction of approximately 5% through a combination of attrition and involuntary layoffs, with notifications beginning in December."
Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. Ortberg said the company has been trying to stabilize output at a rate of about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month.

articles.title_orig: White House cautiously upbeat about Russia-Ukraine peace talks this week
articles.title_zh: White House cautiously upbeat about Russia-Ukraine peace talks this week
articles.content_orig:
A fresh round of peace talks between the US, Ukraine and Russia are set to begin Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, as the Trump administration renews its drive to end the nearly five-year conflict even after it announced significant concessions to Moscow.
Russia has made clear it wants the negotiations – the first of their kind since February – to be strictly trilateral, though national security advisers from several European nations, as well as officials from NATO and the European Union, are also expected in the UAE capital for separate meetings.
“We are working hard to find a negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine,” US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and US negotiator Jared Kushner said Monday.
US officials on Monday underlined that posture, saying that the upcoming talks are a new starting point in defining an end to the war, including discussions on security guarantees and a “post-war security architecture.”
“We need to come up with a way that, when we end this war, it really is a final end to the war, and we believe that’s what Ukraine wants. We believe that’s what Europe wants and we believe that’s what Russia wants,” one official said.
However, many – particularly in Europe – have cast doubt on Moscow’s intentions. The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said Monday she saw little sign that Russia was willing to negotiate in good faith.
Meanwhile, the US official also said that it would be up to Trump to decide whether to offer a US security guarantee as part of peace talks.
The US will be represented by Kushner and Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff, while Ukraine’s foreign intelligence chief and top negotiator Rustem Umerov will lead the Ukrainian delegation, according to the official with knowledge of the talks.
Russia is sending deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin as delegates, according to Russian state news agency TASS, as well as Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov and member of general staff Yuri Zhigarlovsky.
Representatives from the E4 group – the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Italy – as well as officials from NATO and the European Commission will also be in Abu Dhabi, Umerov said Monday. “We will hold separate coordination meetings with our European partners,” Umerov added.
Asked about the presence of European officials in Abu Dhabi, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Monday that Europe has its own channels of communication with Kyiv and Washington, while reaffirming that the talks are “a trilateral negotiation – involving Russia and Ukraine – with the United States acting as a mediator.”
Notably, these talks come amid a renewed push by European nations for a more active role in negotiations over Ukraine’s future, and the security of the bloc at large, after Trump touted a new security deal for Ukraine that “might involve all of Europe.”
“The Europeans will be well represented,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot told French media Sunday. “In recent weeks, the Europeans have made their voices heard. They have expressed to the American mediator that no discussion affecting the future of the continent can ignore our expectations and demands,” he added.
Europe has long been wary of any US-brokered peace deal negotiated without its involvement, with Umerov saying Monday that Ukraine was “doing everything we can to ensure that Europe is a participant in the diplomatic process.”
While the talks will remain trilateral, Kushner said that he and Witkoff would also meet with European partners to continue the “close consultation and coordination we have undertaken on European security and Ukraine’s postwar future over the past several weeks.”
“Ultimately, achieving a comprehensive and lasting settlement will also require direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them,” Kushner posted on X.
This will be the fourth round of trilateral talks. All have ended without significant breakthrough.
Earlier this year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the most recent trilateral talks in Geneva, Switzerland, in February fell short of Ukraine’s goals, saying “sensitive political matters, issues of possible compromises and the necessary meeting of leaders have not yet been sufficiently worked through.”
The US later postponed a round of trilateral talks that were expected to take place in March due to the war in Iran.
Putin is still making maximalist demands previously rejected by Kyiv, including Russian control over Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, a reduction in the size of Ukraine’s military and the abandonment of Kyiv’s ambitions to join NATO.
John Herbst, senior director of the Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center and a former US ambassador to Ukraine, said any expectations for the Abu Dhabi talks should be “very modest.”
“They are only taking place because Putin wants to give Trump a reason to continue to distance himself from Ukraine,” Herbst wrote last week .
With Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine now in its fifth year and gains on the battlefield remaining difficult to come by, Moscow has escalated its aerial attacks – with deadly results for Ukrainians.
At least 55 people were killed last Monday when Russia dropped several bombs on a school building used as a shelter and aid center in Zaporizhzhia , marking one of the deadliest single incidents of the war to date. Civilian deaths in Ukraine are at their highest point since the start of the war, with more than 2,700 killed in Russian strikes so far this year, according to ACLED, a global conflict monitor.
And continuing a pattern seen in previous years, Russian drones and missiles are already hitting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, but harder and earlier than in other winters, analysts say. Russian attacks on the power grid left more than 600,000 people in the Dnipropetrovsk region without electricity overnight into Sunday, Zelensky said, as temperatures plummet and winter draws in.
Over the past few months, Russia has deployed faster, jet-powered Shahed drones, which are harder to shoot down. At the same time, more missiles are slipping through Ukraine’s air defenses as Kyiv grapples with a chronic shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors that are one of the few defensive weapons capable of shooting down ballistic missiles.
Where the Biden administration positioned the US as Ukraine’s biggest single donor and most powerful ally, the Trump administration’s relationship with Kyiv has been decidedly more complicated. It halted financial aid to Ukraine at the beginning of 2025, while the intelligence and technology support it still provides has come under strain in recent weeks too.
Last month, Zelensky accused his Western allies of not providing intelligence warnings before multiple ballistic missile attacks, a claim that the Trump administration denied.
In October too, Ukraine’s ability to use Starshield, a military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink service that is critical to its military operations, was hampered when speed limits were imposed on the satellite terminals. Trump denied approving that decision, while Musk said the Trump administration was behind the ban in a social media post.
Undergirding all this recent tension has been Trump’s sensitivity to rising gas prices, which skyrocketed due to the Iran war and contributed to the Republicans’ landslide defeat in last week’s midterms.
He has shown a willingness to strike business deals with Moscow, including one to supply markets with Russia’s diesel, in a sharp break from the sanctions aimed at punishing and isolating the Russian economy, and pressured Zelensky to accept a short-lived “energy ceasefire.”

articles.title_orig: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
articles.title_zh: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
articles.content_orig:
The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026.
Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect.
In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife.
The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models.
"Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.
Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand.
It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them.
The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little.
But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately.
For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech.
"President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year.
It think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way.
The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others.
We don't know when their affair began or ended , but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work.
China denies that she was engaged in espionage.
Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies.
China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest.
Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations.
Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy.
He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him.
Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients.
At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus.
Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either.
An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one.
And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out.
Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy.
He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.
While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings.
And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.

articles.content_orig:

NASA wants a base on the Moon, and Wall Street is suddenly buying the ride there. Space stocks ripped for a second session Monday as SpaceX ( SPCX ) and seven other companies line up for lunar delivery work worth up to $10 billion.
NASA named the eight winners on Nov. 7 at Kennedy Space Center. Alongside SpaceX and Blue Origin are three smaller public companies, Intuitive Machines ( LUNR ), Firefly Aerospace ( FLY ) and Voyager Technologies ( VOYG ).
For those three, the prize is out of this world. They're worth about $8.5 billion combined, less than the contract's ceiling, though each still has to win missions one by one.
Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) is NASA's way of hiring private companies to fly cargo to the moon. The new 10-year version covers larger landers, and NASA raised the original contract's value to $4.2 billion from $2.6 billion. Intuitive Machines CEO Steve Altemus said the company is "excited to participate in this next evolution of CLPS."
"We are building the Moon Base mission by mission," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in the agency's announcement.
Rocket Lab ( RKLB ) didn't make NASA's list but jumped anyway ahead of its third quarter results after Monday's close. The stock rose about 28% over two sessions, its third-best two-day run in two years, by Yahoo Finance calculations.
Space stocks surged off last week's post-election low, rising roughly 20% to 60% since the Nov. 5 close, with Firefly in the lead. SpaceX posted its biggest two-day gain since early October, while the Nasdaq ( ^IXIC ) gained about 4%.
The bounce follows a brutal stretch. An average of nine space stocks more than doubled this year by May 28, two weeks before SpaceX's June 12 debut, then gave it all back. The group is now down for 2026.
SpaceX is a different story. Wall Street prices it less as a lunar trucker than as an AI cloud, competing with neoclouds — companies like CoreWeave ( CRWV ) that rent out AI computing power — and with hyperscalers, the cloud giants such as Amazon ( AMZN ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ).
On Monday, SpaceX added more than $100 billion in market value, more than the roughly $90 billion that 16 other US-listed space stocks are worth combined. NASA's 10-year moon pot is about a tenth of that one-day gain.
Rocket Lab's third quarter revenue jumped 73% from a year earlier to nearly $268 million, topping estimates, and its fourth quarter forecast came in above Wall Street's. Even so, the stock slipped after hours, and Neutron , its bigger rocket, isn't set to debut until 2027.
The Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman thinks SpaceX's biggest opportunity is back on Earth. Speaking on Yahoo Finance's "Market Hang" on Oct. 30, he said, "They could come out of next year being not only the biggest neocloud, but the largest hyperscaler."

articles.title_orig: Israeli opposition eyes deal with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties to oust Netanyahu
articles.title_zh: Israeli opposition eyes deal with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties to oust Netanyahu
articles.content_orig:
Avigdor Liberman's 2018 haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription proposal has reemerged as a potential basis for coalition negotiations after the Yisrael Beytenu chairman signaled on Sunday that he was willing to compromise with ultra-Orthodox parties. But how does the proposal compare with the draft legislation promoted by Boaz Bismuth in 2025, and would either framework meet the IDF's growing manpower needs?
The 2018 proposal, developed by the Defense Ministry and the IDF during Liberman's tenure as defense minister, sought to gradually increase haredi enlistment while preserving military service deferrals for yeshiva students. It established annual recruitment targets, financial penalties for institutions that failed to meet them, and a mechanism that could ultimately terminate the special exemption arrangement if recruitment targets were repeatedly missed.
Unlike Bismuth's proposal, which introduced additional personal sanctions against individual yeshiva students, Liberman's framework primarily targeted yeshiva funding and the continued validity of the exemption system itself. It also set a lower exemption age of 24, compared with 26 under Bismuth's proposal.
The differences have taken on renewed political significance as Gadi Eisenkot prepares to receive the mandate to form a government. Liberman's decision to lift his veto on cooperation with haredi parties has opened the door to coalition negotiations, although he maintains that his willingness to compromise does not amount to abandoning his support for universal conscription.
"Willingness to compromise does not mean abandoning values and principles," Liberman wrote in a statement on Sunday, defending his change in political position amid criticism from commentators and journalists.
He emphasized that his 2018 proposal would require adjustments in light of the October 7 attacks and the subsequent increase in the military's manpower requirements.
"It is clear to me that following the events of October 7, the law I proposed in 2018 also requires changes and adjustments, but it still constitutes a suitable basis for reaching agreements," he wrote.
Liberman's 2018 legislation was developed by a committee comprising representatives of the Defense Ministry and the IDF. It passed its first reading in the Knesset in July of that year.
The proposal aimed to increase military enlistment among ultra-Orthodox men without dismantling the existing yeshiva system. It allowed many students to continue deferring their service while establishing gradually increasing recruitment targets.
Bismuth's 2025 proposal similarly preserved the possibility of service deferrals and exemptions but added personal restrictions intended to encourage enlistment.
Neither proposal established an immediate and equal military conscription requirement for all young haredi men.
One of the most significant differences between the proposals concerned the age at which yeshiva students could receive exemptions from military service. Liberman's framework set the exemption age at 24, while Bismuth's proposed legislation raised it to 26.
The enforcement mechanisms also differed substantially.
Under Liberman's framework, annual recruitment targets were accompanied by financial sanctions against yeshivas if those targets were not met.
The proposal's most consequential provision addressed prolonged failures to meet recruitment quotas. If actual enlistment remained below 85% of the annual target for three consecutive years, the amendment to the law would expire after an additional 12 months.
This meant that the special arrangement allowing military service deferrals and exemptions could not continue indefinitely if recruitment targets were repeatedly missed.
However, Liberman's proposal did not establish a new system of personal sanctions against individual yeshiva students who failed to enlist.
Instead, its enforcement mechanisms focused primarily on financial penalties for religious institutions and the continued validity of the exemption system.
The committee that developed the framework also recommended expanding administrative sanctions against deserters and draft evaders.
Bismuth's proposal, by contrast, introduced personal sanctions alongside financial penalties for yeshivas that failed to comply with the law.
Those proposed restrictions included limitations on overseas travel, obtaining a new driver's license before age 23, and eligibility for certain government benefits and economic incentives.
However, the personal sanctions were not all designed to take effect automatically or immediately.
Some depended on the issuance of an enlistment order and the individual's subsequent failure to report for duty. Others were linked to failures to meet broader recruitment targets, while certain restrictions were subject to age limits or delayed implementation dates.
The proposal also included provisions allowing sanctions to be eased or exemptions to be granted under specified circumstances.
For individual yeshiva students, Bismuth's framework was therefore more stringent because it introduced additional personal restrictions.
On the exemption system as a whole, however, Liberman's proposal established a potentially more far-reaching consequence for persistent failures to meet recruitment targets.
Under his framework, the special legislative arrangement could expire following three consecutive years of missed targets, subject to the stipulated 12-month transition period.
Bismuth's proposal included review mechanisms, financial sanctions, and possible adjustments, but did not establish an equivalent automatic mechanism terminating the entire exemption arrangement.
The differences are also evident in the recruitment targets themselves.
Liberman's framework established a target of 3,996 recruits in 2018, gradually increasing to 4,967 in 2021 and 6,208 in 2025.
One version of Bismuth's framework set a target of 8,160 recruits over 18 months, averaging about 5,440 per year.
Under that version, up to 10% of the recruitment target could be met by individuals performing civilian service in security-related fields.
At first glance, Bismuth's initial target appears higher than the target Liberman established for 2018. However, Bismuth's annual average was lower than the target Liberman's proposal established for 2025.
The figures do not represent identical periods or legislative arrangements operating under equivalent timetables.
Several versions of the recruitment targets were presented during the advancement of Bismuth's framework. Each figure must therefore be examined in light of the specific legislative version and period it refers to.
Another significant difference concerns how recruits are counted.
Liberman's framework established targets for national and civilian service separately from military enlistment targets.
Under one version of Bismuth's proposal, civilian service in security-related fields could count toward the overall recruitment quota, up to 10% of the target.
Consequently, meeting the overall quota would not necessarily indicate that an equivalent number of new soldiers had joined the IDF.
The identity of those included in the recruitment figures has also sparked controversy.
One criticism of Bismuth's framework concerned the possibility of counting young men who had already left the haredi community.
If a young man raised in the ultra-Orthodox community but no longer studying at a yeshiva is counted as a haredi recruit, meeting the recruitment target does not necessarily demonstrate increased enlistment among students attending active yeshivas.
Beyond these legal and numerical differences lies a fundamental change in Israel's security requirements.
Liberman's proposal was developed in 2018, five years before the October 7 attacks and the war that followed.
Since then, the haredi population has grown, while the IDF's manpower requirements have increased significantly.

articles.title_orig: Silicon Valley’s Trump-era playbook is falling apart. A major shift is underway.
articles.title_zh: Silicon Valley’s Trump-era playbook is falling apart. A major shift is underway.
articles.content_orig:
Democrats won seats on anti-datacentre tickets and Musk wasted nearly half a billion dollars. Big tech may be losing its grip, but it won’t go quietly
P hotos That Precede Unfortunate Events: a couple of months back, Donald Trump hosted some of the world’s most powerful tech executives at the White House for a “ Super Intelligence luncheon ”, which by coincidence is also how my mum described her tuna sandwiches in a forlorn attempt to get me to eat them. Sitting either side of the president were Elon Musk, making a rare offline appearance in daylight hours, and Jensen Huang, the Nvidia chief executive carving out a precious slot in what we now know was an extremely busy schedule.
Over a delicious meal of microchips and rare-earth metals, the billionaires sketched out a utopian future of an AI industry unencumbered by regulation or safeguards, powered by their heroic strongman leader, a political genius effortlessly able to impose his will upon an entire nation. And perhaps it should have been apparent even at the time that these (mostly) men were putting their faith in a guy who had recently been defeated by pond algae . But as the drinks and the good times flowed, it was still possible to believe that the sun would never set on the thousand-year American superintelligence empire.
And so, while we’re all learning lessons from the resounding defeat delivered to Trumpism last week, might we start with a modest and sober reassessment of the Silicon Valley oligarch class? For years, we have been told that these are some of humanity’s greatest seers and visionaries, the Leonardos and Einsteins of the 21st century, the people best placed to plot a course for our species, despite for the most part not being able to smile without looking as though they were undergoing a juice enema.
As it turned out, this small band of brilliant clairvoyants somehow failed to anticipate the possibility that the deeply unpopular man they were clasping in a tender embrace would be subjected to an absolute democracy-mogging in just a few weeks, throwing their altruistic wet dreams into chaos. After all, last week’s midterms were not simply a rebuke to one man or one party, but to an entire ideology. Across the US, voters took their revenge not just on big tech, but on the politicians who had enabled it.
In Texas, Gina Hinojosa beat the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott, by promising an immediate moratorium on datacentre development, and despite being outspent almost eight to one, in large part by big tech donors desperate to preserve their tax breaks. In Ohio, the Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown described his opponent, Jon Husted, as “the face of datacentres”, a visually horrifying concept. In total, 46 of the 47 ballot measures relating to datacentres were defeated . By Thursday morning, the markets had responded with a devastating sell-off of tech stocks , the repercussions of which are still shaking out as you read this.
Should we read anything into the fact that the biggest progressive landslide in 52 years, catalysed by a concerted mobilisation of Black, Latino and young voters, was sufficient to send the financial markets into existential panic? Anyone able to join the dots for us there? Is it relevant that the São Paulo stock exchange plunged about 14% after Lula da Silva’s shock election victory in Brazil last month? Just what is it about the popular repudiation of hard-right autocrats that appears to spook the pillars of capitalism so much?
For the time being, big tech does not appear to be as politically polarising in Britain as it is in the US. This is largely because much of the recent acceleration has occurred under a Labour administration, in particular under the late lamented Keir Starmer, a prime minister who in retrospect may actually have been a semi-sentient chatbot all along. “We will test and understand AI before we regulate it,” Starmer once said, which he appears to have done by plugging it directly into his own mouth for two years. But this is an issue that will continue to rise in democratic salience, in part because it relies on the undemocratic manufacture of consent, an inexorable march deliberately designed to circumvent scrutiny.
after newsletter promotion
Take the UK government’s AI growth zones , designed to supercharge datacentre development by taking decisions on nationally significant infrastructure projects (NSIP) away from local councils. A recent report by Spotlight on Corruption found that over two years, ministers met only two community groups and no environmental organisations while developing the policy, while at the same time ministers and senior civil servants were hired to 38 roles at AI companies. Naturally, you are likely to hear very little opposition to any of this, either from the billionaire-owned press or the official opposition; indeed, Kemi Badenoch is perhaps the only major party leader you can imagine typing “what do I think of AI” into an AI prompt.
You will occasionally hear the assumption, made on both sides of the Atlantic and often on the flimsiest of evidence, that voters are increasingly fed up with democracy. But what if we’re getting this the wrong way round? What if, in fact, it is those who are supposed to be upholding democracy – the politicians and media and captains of industry, all slowly stewing in X-brained algorithmic talking points – who are beginning to tire of it? While Musk spends enormous chunks of his fortune trying (and failing) to tip the electoral scales in favour of the hard right, Reform UK rakes in £72m in donations from two cryptocurrency billionaires. Bonus question: do we think the brave men and women out there on the tech frontier will respond to democratic setbacks by demanding more democratic accountability, or less?
And, of course, in these febrile and fragile times you have to take your wins wherever you get them. But as any ChatGPT user will tell you, making bold claims on the basis of a bare minimum of data is always an exercise fraught with risk. Saying no once will never be enough. In a note to investors last week, Goldman Sachs wrote: “We expect the datacentre issue to somewhat fade in importance and any moratoria on datacentre development to be short-lived.” You can decide for yourself what it means by that.

articles.content_orig:
Lucid Group missed Wall Street's third-quarter expectations as the embattled electric vehicle maker continues an "operational reset" aimed at cutting costs and narrowing losses.
The company on Monday also announced a $1.75 billion increase in a delayed draw term loan from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, the company's largest shareholder.
Lucid stock fell roughly 5% in aftermarket trading Monday.
Here's how Lucid performed in the third quarter compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:
Despite the top- and bottom-line misses, the company's adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of a loss of $726 million beat Wall Street's expectations of a loss of $611 million for the third quarter. Its net loss for the quarter was $830.9 million, down from a loss of $978.4 million a year earlier.
Lucid's 2025 third quarter included revenue of $336.6 million, a loss of $3.31 per share and an adjusted EBITDA loss of $717.7 million.
The quarterly results are the first since Lucid CEO Silvio Napoli , who started leading the company in June, announced a restructuring plan that included implementing several cost-cutting efforts and delaying the company's upcoming midsize vehicle from the end of this year until the second half of next.
"Our transformation is beginning to show progress. We are acting with urgency, strengthening the fundamentals and driving greater discipline, while continuing to invest in the priorities to deliver profitable long-term growth," Napoli said in a release.
The company's turnaround plan includes $1.4 billion in cash flow improvements this year as well as focusing attention on a robotaxi program with Uber and Nuro, a factory that's under construction in Saudi Arabia and the midsize vehicle.
Lucid said the capital from PIF is expected to give the company "additional financial flexibility as Lucid delivers on its turnaround program." It is expected to assist in funding "operations and key investments" into the fourth quarter of 2027, including the start of production for the midsize vehicle.
The additional funds boost Lucid's total liquidity to $3.75 billion, up from $2 billion to end the third quarter.
"We are grateful for the continued financial support from our anchor shareholder, which further energizes us to remain focused on execution and on our commitments as we build a stronger, sustainable Lucid," Napoli said.
Lucid said Monday that the company expects to communicate its midterm plan and targets early next year. The EV maker in May suspended its guidance and many targets, citing new leadership and time needed to develop a turnaround plan.

articles.title_orig: A Sam Altman parody offers an amusing lesson in memory management
articles.title_zh: A Sam Altman parody offers an amusing lesson in memory management
articles.content_orig:
Sam Altman’s recent comments on the Cheeky Pint podcast inspired developer Iain Kay to create a satirical script that allows users to email the OpenAI CEO once per day if more than 10 percent of their system RAM is reported as available. Ram-Altman is described by its creator as a “parody project” launched in response to Altman’s viral remarks about RAM in your personal PC.
As reported by The Verge , on the October 29 episode recorded with Stripe President John Collison, Altman said, “A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center. But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5 percent of the time.”
Altman has since explained that his comments were taken out of context and briefly changed his display name to “RAM Altman” on X, which Kay calls on the project GitHub, “objectively excellent and where the project gets its name.”
In an email to Ars, Kay said, “Ram-Altman is a bash script that takes MemTotal minus MemAvailable from /proc/meminfo, so the figure includes page cache and reclaimable slab but leaves out tmpfs and shared memory.”
If the script only showed what Linux reports as “free” RAM, it would paint an incomplete picture. Linux often reports a surprisingly small amount of “free” RAM, as it doesn’t count memory that is currently claimable for use. Linux will fill available RAM caches with file data for quick access, but the kernel can reclaim that usage at a moment’s notice when needed. The MemAvailable figure is the kernel’s own estimate of how much memory it could hand over without swapping.
Users can schedule the script to ask the kernel for a status update every five minutes, and if more than 10 percent of RAM is available, it triggers a joke email from one of several joke templates. The script limits outgoing emails to one per day.
The GitHub page for the RAM-Altman project includes a dry-run option that any Linux user with a Bash terminal should be able to paste and run without the need for email trolling. When the threshold is exceeded, each dry run output features one generated joke email, so repeated runs produce different amusing examples.
A test run of the script on my Fedora 44 KDE machine confirmed the author’s measurements. Inside the System – Info Center of my Fedora desktop, the system reports 14.9 GiB of total usable system RAM after the kernel and firmware take their needed slices of the 16 GiB of physical memory. This reflects the total amount of capacity the system has to work with, not the amount available at any given time. The Ram-Altman script shows that of that 14.9 GiB total pool, 10 GiB is used, with 4.9 GiB available (33.1 percent). That figure isn’t the simple sum of the “free” and “cache” lines that the script displays, but a kernel-calculated figure that accounts for the full amount of memory that can be reclaimed.
The project concedes the nuance that Altman was referring to how much time memory spends being utilized, while the script measures how much capacity is free at the time of measurement. While the script might tell Altman that 33 percent of your system RAM is available, it doesn’t outline how often that’s the case. The concession steps on the joke slightly, but it keeps everyone honest.
The GitHub is wise to point out that “ --dry-run is the best way to enjoy this. It costs nothing and all the jokes are there.” Used irresponsibly, this cheeky joke could morph into a harassment tool, and Kay quickly points out that the script does not include anyone’s email, including Altman’s. Users who deploy their own operating version are encouraged to only use their own real email addresses and honor any requests to stop, as is outlined at the bottom of the script-generated output.
If you’re interested in taking a look at some of the emails generated without having to spin up a Linux machine that reports the system status every five minutes, the ram-altman.lol project website rotates through sample emails generated by the script. Kay writes on the website that, “In fairness, he says the remarks were taken out of context , posted ‘i want you to have so much ram’ , and briefly went by Ram Altman on X. That makes this script a daily progress report.”

articles.title_orig: Who is Alice Huang, the woman linked to Nvidia’s CEO?
articles.title_zh: Who is Alice Huang, the woman linked to Nvidia’s CEO?
articles.content_orig:
CEO reportedly ‌had close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing
Nvidia said ⁠on Sunday it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.
The New York Times reported in ​October that Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence that Huang ‌had a close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump downplayed the revelations about Huang, who is an influential adviser to the president on artificial intelligence, saying: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.”
Trump also brushed off a question about whether he now regrets not acting on the intelligence when he was briefed on it, and suggested that he would be happy to take Huang with him on a trip to Asia next week. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody. But, you know, so does everybody else.”
Republican lawmakers have expressed more alarm, asking Huang to give the House foreign affairs and intelligence committees a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and his relationship with Alice Huang or Huang Le, an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed, who is of no relation to the Nvidia CEO. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her.
Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
The company’s board said in a statement on Sunday that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information.
“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”
Huang fully ‌supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, it added.
Axios reported on ​Sunday, citing a draft email by Huang to employees, that Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and took full ⁠responsibility for his actions.
“I was unfaithful to my ​wife. My ​actions hurt her ​and our children. There is no excuse ​for what ‌I did,” ​Huang said ​in the draft email also seen by Reuters.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Axios report.
The Times reported on Sunday that a memo drafted by US secretary of state Marco Rubio circulated among top policymakers in the Trump administration last spring, citing intelligence that the businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive was a spy for China’s ministry of state security. Despite those concerns, Huang was invited to join Trump’s delegation when he traveled to China in May. Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, were also invited to a state dinner at the White House in September for Xi Jinping and seated at the top table with Trump and China’s president.
Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom, placing Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
However, national security concerns have prompted strict US export controls, effectively barring the company from selling its top-tier processors to customers in China.
US officials have cited threats to the US supply chain and fears over national security risks as a rationale for the restrictions. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, has also suggested that China could be sanctioned for theft of US data and intellectual property.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Alice Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
The investigation also follows a rough few days on Wall Street for AI tech firms, particularly Nvidia. A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings led to a total decline of nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.
A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward recently.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO’s Moment of Truth Nears as Waiting Period Expires
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO’s Moment of Truth Nears as Waiting Period Expires
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic's upcoming initial public offering could be a crucial test of investor confidence in the artificial intelligence trade, CNBC's Jim Cramer said on Monday.
"Without it, I don't see how the AI-related stocks can make a real recovery," the " Mad Money " host said, exactly two weeks after the Claude developer filed its S-1 IPO paperwork. Despite the recent sell-off in AI stocks, Anthropic is reportedly moving ahead with its IPO plans. The company is expected to meet with major investors this week and is targeting a trading debut as early as Thursday or Friday of next week, the Wall Street Journal reported , citing people familiar with the matter. "I don't think it's hyperbolic to say that this could be one of the most consequential IPOs in history."
Cramer explained that the billions of dollars being spent on AI chips and data centers ultimately depend on a handful of AI developers, including Anthropic, generating enough revenue to justify those investments.
"Anthropic is important because it is one of just a few companies at the end of the food chain for all of the AI data center investments that we've seen, so it is one of the few companies that, ultimately, needs to make money from all of this investment spending," Cramer said. "If it can't do that, or if it cannot convince enough investors that it will do so, then it's tough to justify all of the AI investments that are being made today."
Cramer pointed to SpaceX as an example of how interconnected the AI trade has become. Much of the Elon Musk rocket and AI company's recent revenue growth has come from renting computing capacity to customers, including Alphabet's Google and Anthropic. Google pays roughly $900 million a month for that capacity, while Anthropic's commitment has grown from an initial $1.25 billion monthly to more than $3 billion, according to its IPO prospectus.
Those contracts allow for SpaceX's massive purchases of Nvidia chips. "But if an Anthropic deal fails?" Cramer said. "Then Anthropic wouldn't have the cash to fulfill its contracts, and you'd have to take down estimates for both SpaceX and Nvidia, along with a whole host of other compute providers to Anthropic, and their suppliers." Not to mention, Alphabet, Amazon , and Nvidia have all invested in Anthropic, making their earnings sensitive to changes in the AI developer's valuation.
The wrinkle here is that investor appetite for an Anthropic IPO appears to be weakening. Anthropic's potential valuation has reportedly fallen from as much as $2 trillion earlier this fall to as low as $1 trillion following last week's technology sell-off on concerns that the Democratic wave in the midterm election will mean slower new data center construction.
On Friday, during the CNBC Investing Club's Annual Meeting , Cramer also stressed the importance of the Anthropic offering to the AI trade and to Club portfolio names Alphabet, Amazon and Nvidia.

articles.title_orig: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
articles.title_zh: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
articles.content_orig:
France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers across the country last month.
Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding those who were responsible would be hit with sanctions.
Iran has yet to respond officially, but some Iranian media outlets have dismissed the allegations as baseless.
The French hacking, which led to the destruction of tons of frozen and chilled food in France was followed by a similar attack against supermarkets across several other European countries. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".
He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".
France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.
The Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with the IRGC as well as his two deputies.
Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime.
In recent weeks, a number of commentators and politicians in Iran have argued that the country should extend any retaliation beyond the Middle East if the US and Israel resume the war they started earlier this year.
If the IRGC carried out the cyber-attacks, it remains unclear whether they were part of Iran's deterrence strategy.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.
More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.
Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.
The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.
Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe.
Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in countries including Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Separately in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction, spoiling food. This incident is also being investigated as deliberate cyber-attacks, Reuters news agency has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.
In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.
The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber-attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.

articles.title_orig: China extends pause on rare earth export curbs for two months
articles.title_zh: China extends pause on rare earth export curbs for two months
articles.content_orig:
China on Monday announced it is suspending export controls on some critical minerals for two months, preserving a broader trade deal struck between Washington and Beijing before an expected meeting between presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Asia next week.
The announcement from China's Ministry of Commerce formalises an agreement to extend a bilateral trade truce that was set to expire on Tuesday. The extension runs to January 10, according to the ministry. China's finance ministry also said a 24 per cent tariff on US goods would be suspended for two months, although it will still charge a 10 per cent fee, according to a statement.
A filing from the Office of the US Trade Representative posted in the Federal Register also said it was suspending action from a Section 301 investigation into China 's maritime and logistic sectors. The US is also extending 178 current Section 301 tariff exclusions for Chinese goods, according to a second filing.
Where does Trump's critical minerals strategy go from here?
China announced a package of export controls on seven heavy rare earth elements last April, before expanding that list in October. It had earlier announced export curbs on battery supply chain chokepoints, including cathode materials, cathode precursors and graphite anode materials, widening a trade rift with Washington and stoking fears of a potential global supply chain crisis .
China accounted for 60 per cent of global mined production of magnet rare earths in 2024 and 91 per cent of global refined output, according to the International Energy Agency. It holds an even higher share for permanent magnet production.
The US and China entered into a one-year trade truce last October during their summit in Busan, South Korea, that paused tit-for-tat tariff measures, deferred rare earth curbs and included a pledge from China to resume importing US soybeans.
However, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last week urged Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng to “fully and immediately” implement its commitments in Busan, while also raising concerns about “recent Chinese actions”, his department said in a statement.
In a separate statement, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said it remained important for China to fully implement its commitments, particularly in relation to agricultural purchases, rare earths and other critical minerals.
“There is an effort that has been co-ordinated between Treasury and the White House to track various commitments made by China since they first met in Busan,” said a former senior US official. “It's not just critical minerals; it is purchases of various agricultural products, where they stand on GE engines and Boeing,”
“And I think there are people … inside the US government that believe that China has overpromised and underdelivered, and they are making a consistent case that the issue that Bessent and Greer went out on was on critical minerals.”
Meanwhile, China said it “expressed serious concern” over recent US restrictions after Washington placed sanctions on two Chinese companies over their alleged ties to the Cuban regime's oil shipping networks supporting the Cuban military.
Mr Trump and Mr Xi are expected to hold a meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit held in Shenzhen next week. It would be the leaders' third meeting this year.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE:BRKA)(NYSE:BRKB) has never spent this much on its own stock in one quarter. The company spent about $9.6 billion on repurchases in the third quarter of 2026. This inches past the nearly $9.3 billion it spent in the third quarter of 2020.
At Berkshire, a buyback also says something about price. The company repurchases shares only if management thinks they cost less than the business is worth.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
And the Class B shares now trade near $570 as I write, about 12% over the average price Berkshire paid in September. I think the record buyback says a lot about what the stock was worth then, and a lot less about what it's worth at today's price.
Warren Buffett. Image source: Getty Images.
Warren Buffett , now Berkshire's chairman emeritus, spelled out his rule for repurchases in his 2011 letter to shareholders.
"Charlie and I favor repurchases when two conditions are met: first, a company has ample funds to take care of the operational and liquidity needs of its business; second, its stock is selling at a material discount to the company's intrinsic business value, conservatively calculated," he wrote, referring to his late partner, Charlie Munger.
Intrinsic value is an estimate of what a whole business is worth.
Versions of both tests remain in Berkshire's latest quarterly filing, which says it can repurchase shares whenever its CEO, after consulting the chairman of the board, "believes that the repurchase price is below Berkshire's intrinsic value, conservatively determined." These two roles now belong to Greg Abel and Howard Buffett, Warren's son.
Berkshire also won't buy back stock if doing so would push its cash and Treasury bills below $30 billion. And it had around $352 billion in both insurance and other businesses at the end of September, so the first test isn't a big hurdle.
The program no longer has a set price limit, though. Until 2018, Berkshire wouldn't pay over a 20% premium to book value (what's left after subtracting a company's liabilities from its assets). Based on a book value of about $358 per Class B share at the end of September, that limit would be roughly $429, well under the stock's 52-week low of about $464. So, Berkshire is buying at prices the old valuation limit wouldn't have allowed.
Showing how fast the buying has accelerated, Berkshire repurchased no stock in 2025. Then it bought around $235 million in the first quarter of 2026 and about $4.5 billion in the second quarter.
Across both share classes, Berkshire spent around $3.4 billion in July at an average of about $496 per Class B share, about $847 million in August at about $504, and about $5.4 billion in September at around $507. So its biggest month of buying came at its highest average price of the quarter.
The buying also seems to have kept going. Berkshire's share count dropped by the equivalent of about 3.8 million Class B shares from Sept. 30 to Oct. 28, suggesting about $2 billion more in buybacks. The filing doesn't give prices for those weeks, when the Class B shares closed between about $501 and $549.
A buyback signals to investors that the CEO believed the shares were worth more than the price paid. It doesn't say how much more. Sure, "conservatively determined" suggests the full value might be well above what Berkshire paid. But the company doesn't publish its estimate.
Today's buyer pays around 15% more than Berkshire's July average. That's a valuation of about 1.6 times book value at the end of September, up from around 1.4 times book value at September's average price.
The third quarter's numbers don't explain the stock's run-up since September, either. Berkshire's third-quarter operating earnings (which leave out the swings in its stock portfolio that skew net income) dropped around 6% year over year to about $12.7 billion. Without foreign-currency effects on Berkshire's debt, they dropped less than 1%. But insurance underwriting earnings fell about 43%.
At roughly $570, the stock trades at about 26 times last 12 months' operating earnings.
In the end, I think the record buyback is a strong sign that about $507 was a good price for Berkshire stock, and a far weaker one than about $570 is.
I'd still consider buying near $570, given how much cash Berkshire has left to deploy. But I'd be a lot more interested at prices closer to what Berkshire itself paid.
